## 2.a: Research Question


## 2.b: Classification Research Question
Which classifier, kNN or Naive Bayes, can more accurately predict a pitch result (ball/strike/in play) from pre-pitch information such as pitch type, ball-strike count, velocity, spin rate, horizontal/vertical break, and pitcher/batter handedness?

The target is the Statcast pitch result `type`, with $K = 3$ classes: `Ball` (B), `Strike` (S), and `InPlay` (X). Predicting pitch results matters because it lets pitchers, catchers, and defenses anticipate what a given pitch is likely to produce. Below is a table with all variables and a connection to the EDA done previously. All plot names refer to the EDA from Nadolski_Group_Exercise1.

|Variable|Type|Justification|
|--|--|-----|
|Pitch Type| Categorical|Plot 1: Strike percentage differ by pitch type|
|Balls| Numerical|Plot 3: Pitch type differs by ball-strike count.|
|Strikes| Numerical|Plot 3: Pitch type differs by ball-strike count.|
|Velocity| Numerical|Plot 4: Velocity differs by pitch outcome (Ball, Foul, other).|
|Spin Rate| Numerical|Table 2: Spin differs by pitch type.|
|Horizontal Break| Numerical|Table 2: Horizontal break differs by pitch type.|
|Vertical Break| Numerical|Table 2: Vertical break differs by pitch type.|
|Pitcher Handedness| Categorical| Domain knowledge, same batter-handedness advantage.|
|Batter Handedness| Categorical| Domain knowledge, opposite pitcher-handedness advantage.|

 \hfill\break

```{r, echo=FALSE}
classes <- c("Ball", "Strike", "InPlay")
classification_data <- baseballData %>%
  transmute(Y = factor(type, levels = c("B", "S", "X"), labels = classes),
            pitch_name = as.character(pitch_name),
            balls, strikes, release_speed, release_spin_rate,
            pfx_x = abs(pfx_x), pfx_z,
            stand = as.character(stand), p_throws = as.character(p_throws))
```


```{r, echo=FALSE}

classification_data <- classification_data[complete.cases(classification_data) &
                                           classification_data$pitch_name != "", ]
n_removed <- n_raw - nrow(classification_data)
```


```{r, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(1234)
# Split data into 80%/20% training/testing split
index <- sample(1:nrow(classification_data), round(nrow(classification_data) * 0.8))
training_df <- classification_data[index, ]
testing_df <- classification_data[-index, ]
```


```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Training class proportions
K <- length(classes)

pi_train <- prop.table(table(training_df$Y))
kable(data.frame(Class = classes, Proportion = round(as.numeric(pi_train), 3)),
      caption = "Training class proportions $\\pi_k$.")
```


```{r, echo=FALSE}
# No-skill model baselines
majority <- names(which.max(pi_train))
null_acc <- mean(testing_df$Y == majority)                              
null_ll <- -mean(log(pi_train[as.character(testing_df$Y)]))
null_ll_train <- -sum(pi_train * log(pi_train))

baselines <- c(accuracy_NIR = max(pi_train),
               balanced_acc = 1 / K,
               MCC = 0,
               log_loss = null_ll_train,
               brier = 1 - sum(pi_train^2))

baseline_tab <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Accuracy", "Balanced accuracy", "MCC",
             "Log-loss", "Brier score"),
  `Training proportions` = round(baselines, 3),
  check.names = FALSE)

kable(baseline_tab, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "No-skill baselines")
```

## 3.a: Data Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention
**Classification**
**Data split:** 
We used an 80/20 train/test split with `set.seed(1234)` and the test set was touched only once, after all tuning was finished.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Combine pitches with <50 training pitches into 'Other' (levels chosen from TRAIN only)
keep <- names(which(table(training_df$pitch_name) >= 50))
collapse_pitch <- function(x) ifelse(x %in% keep, x, "Other")
training_df$pitch_name <- collapse_pitch(training_df$pitch_name)
testing_df$pitch_name  <- collapse_pitch(testing_df$pitch_name)
```

**Rare pitch types:** 
From the EDA, many pitch types appeared very few times. For example, forkball and pitch out have only one observation each. Categories that small make estimates unstable for both models, so pitch types with fewer than 50 training observations were collapsed into an "Other" category. The collapsing rule was performed after the split, so the test set did not influence it.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Turn categorical vars into factors
cat_vars <- c("pitch_name", "stand", "p_throws")
for (v in cat_vars) {
  lv <- sort(unique(training_df[[v]]))
  training_df[[v]] <- factor(training_df[[v]], levels = lv)
  testing_df[[v]]  <- factor(testing_df[[v]],  levels = lv)
}
```

**kNN Standardization:**

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Standardize by z-score

numerical_vars <- c("balls", "strikes", "release_speed", "release_spin_rate", "pfx_x", "pfx_z")
train_scaled <- scale(training_df[, numerical_vars])
center_vals <- attr(train_scaled, "scaled:center")
scale_vals  <- attr(train_scaled, "scaled:scale")
test_scaled <- scale(testing_df[, numerical_vars], center = center_vals, scale = scale_vals)

# Summary table
pretty <- c(balls = "Balls", strikes = "Strikes",
            release_speed = "Release speed", release_spin_rate = "Spin rate",
            pfx_x = "Horizontal break", pfx_z = "Vertical break",
            pitch_name = "Pitch type", stand = "Batter stance", p_throws = "Pitcher handedness")

scale_check <- rbind("Train mean" = colMeans(train_scaled),
                     "Test mean" = colMeans(test_scaled))
colnames(scale_check) <- pretty[colnames(scale_check)]

kable(round(scale_check, 3),
      caption = "Means in the training and test sets. Scaling parameters come from the training set only.")
```

After looking at histograms, boxplots, and qqplots, there are a few outliers in a feature release_spin_rate. Therefore, we will standardize by z-score as it is less sensitive to extreme values.

In the table above, the training set feature means are all close to zero, which is what we want. Further, our testing means are near zero, but not exactly zero. We want this too, as the test set was not used to define "zero." 

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Check is.ordered() to decide nominal/ordinal 
is.ordered(classification_data$stand)
is.ordered(classification_data$p_throws)
is.ordered(classification_data$pitch_name)
```

**Categorical Encoding: kNN encoding:**
Categorical variables pitch_name, stand, and p_throws have no order. There is no ranking among the pitches slider, sinker, changeup, etc. Additionally, there is no order in whether a pitcher is a righty or a lefty. Therefore, they are nominal variables and get dummy encoded.  

Pitch name, batter side, and pitcher hand are dummy coded (1/2) and left unscaled. Balls, strikes, velocity, spin rate, and horizontal/vertical break are z-scored using the training mean and SD, and those same training values are applied to the test set. Inside cross-validation, the mean and SD come from the fitting folds only.

**Categorical Encoding: Naive Bayes encoding:** 
Pitch name, batter side, pitcher hand, balls, and strikes are treated as categorical features with class-conditional frequency tables (Laplace smoothing, $\alpha = 1$). Velocity, spin rate, and horizontal/vertical break use Gaussian class-conditional densities, which is scale invariant. These features are left unstandardized.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
# Encode nominal variables with full one-hot 
one_hot <- function(df) {
  ctr <- lapply(Filter(is.factor, df), function(f) contrasts(f, contrasts = FALSE))
  model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = df, contrasts.arg = ctr)
}

X_train <- cbind(train_scaled, one_hot(training_df[cat_vars]))
X_test <- cbind(test_scaled,  one_hot(testing_df[cat_vars]))
ytr <- as.integer(training_df$Y)

# Test if variable encoding worked
stopifnot(identical(colnames(X_train), colnames(X_test)))
colnames(X_train)
```

**Probability outputs and decision rule:** 
Because the target has $K = 3$ classes, there is no single threshold $\tau$. Both models predict the class with the largest probability, $\hat{y} = \arg\max_k \hat{p}_k(x)$. kNN probabilities are smoothed vote fractions $\hat{p}_k = (\text{votes}_k + 1)/(k + K)$. Naive Bayes probabilities are the posterior class probabilities $\hat{P}(Y = k \mid x)$.The probabilities themselves are used for log-loss and the Brier score, and the argmax predictions are used for the confusion matrices and the threshold-dependent metrics.

## 4.b: Hyperparameter Optimization of kNN: Regression





## 4.c: Hyperparameter Optimization of kNN: Classification
```{r, echo=FALSE}
kmax <- 301
k.grid <- c(seq(1, 51, by = 2), seq(61, kmax, by = 10))

# Class votes
knn_votes <- function(fit.X, fit.y, new.X, kmax) {
  nn <- FNN::get.knnx(fit.X, new.X, k = kmax, algorithm = "brute")$nn.index
  L  <- matrix(fit.y[nn], nrow = nrow(new.X))
  lapply(1:K, function(j) t(apply(L == j, 1, cumsum)))
}
# Laplace-smoothed vote (votes + 1) / (k + K)
smooth_p <- function(votes, k) sapply(1:K, function(j) (votes[[j]][, k] + 1) / (k + K))

multi_log_loss <- function(y, P, eps = 1e-15) {
  P <- pmin(pmax(P, eps), 1 - eps)
  -mean(log(P[cbind(seq_along(y), as.integer(y))]))
}
bal_acc <- function(y, pred) {
  tab <- table(factor(pred, 1:K), factor(y, 1:K))
  mean(diag(tab) / colSums(tab))
}
knn_metrics <- function(votes, y, k) {
  P <- smooth_p(votes, k)
  c(BalancedAcc = bal_acc(y, max.col(P, "random")), LogLoss = multi_log_loss(y, P))
}

# 5-fold CV 
set.seed(1234)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(training_df)))

cv_knn <- function(v) {
  fit <- training_df[folds != v, ];  
  val <- training_df[folds == v, ]
  fit.num <- scale(fit[, numerical_vars])
  val.num <- scale(val[, numerical_vars],
                   center = attr(fit.num, "scaled:center"),
                   scale  = attr(fit.num, "scaled:scale"))
  votes <- knn_votes(cbind(fit.num, one_hot(fit[cat_vars])), as.integer(fit$Y),
                     cbind(val.num, one_hot(val[cat_vars])), kmax)
  t(sapply(k.grid, function(k) knn_metrics(votes, as.integer(val$Y), k)))
}
knn.cv <- data.frame(k = k.grid, Reduce(`+`, lapply(1:5, cv_knn)) / 5)

# Training curve on a 5,000-pitch subsample 
sub       <- sample(nrow(training_df), 5000)
votes_tr  <- knn_votes(X_train, ytr, X_train[sub, ], kmax)
knn.train <- data.frame(k = k.grid,
                        t(sapply(k.grid, function(k) knn_metrics(votes_tr, ytr[sub], k))))

# Choose k*
best_ll <- min(knn.cv$LogLoss)
k_ll <- knn.cv$k[which.min(knn.cv$LogLoss)]
k_star <- min(knn.cv$k[knn.cv$LogLoss <= best_ll + 0.001])
k_ba <- knn.cv$k[which.max(knn.cv$BalancedAcc)]
knn.cv$LL_improvement <- 1 - knn.cv$LogLoss / null_ll_train
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
# Optimization plots
tune_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  rbind(data.frame(set = "5-fold CV", knn.cv[, c("k", "BalancedAcc", "LogLoss")]),
        data.frame(set = "Training",  knn.train)),
  c(BalancedAcc, LogLoss), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value")
ref <- data.frame(metric = c("BalancedAcc", "LogLoss"), value = c(1 / K, null_ll_train))

ggplot(tune_long, aes(k, value, colour = set)) + geom_line() +
  geom_hline(data = ref, aes(yintercept = value), linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = k_star, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Neighborhood size k (log scale)", y = NULL, 
       title = "Optimization Plots",
       colour = NULL)

top <- rbind(cbind(Best = "BA", knn.cv[order(-knn.cv$BalancedAcc), ][1:3, 1:3]),
             cbind(Best = "LL", knn.cv[order(knn.cv$LogLoss), ][1:3, 1:3]),
             cbind(Best = "k*", knn.cv[knn.cv$k == k_star, 1:3]))
kable(top, digits = 4, caption = "Tuning table for optimal k selection.", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
yte <- as.integer(testing_df$Y)

votes_te <- knn_votes(X_train, ytr, X_test, k_star)
P_knn    <- smooth_p(votes_te, k_star)
colnames(P_knn) <- classes

set.seed(99)
pred_knn <- max.col(P_knn, ties.method = "random")
```

We searched neighborhood sizes with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set only. The grid started at $k \in \{1, 3, 5,..., 51\}$. The best CV $k$ landed on the boundary of 51, so the grid was extended to 301 (steps of 10 beyond 51). The log-loss minimum then landed on the new boundary of 301, but the curve is essentially flat beyond $k \approx 100$, so extending the grid further would not change the conclusion. The final $k^* =$ `r k_star` was chosen by cross-validated log-loss, using the smallest $k$ within 0.001 of the minimum because the curve is flat. The minimum log-loss was at $k =$ `r k_ll`, while balanced accuracy peaked much earlier at $k =$ `r k_ba`, so the two metrics did not agree. Balanced accuracy is nearly flat across all $k$ (roughly 0.3576 to 0.3573, against a no-skill value of `r round(1 / K, 3)`), so its differences are too small to be meaningful. Log-loss decided because it is a strictly proper scoring rule that uses the full probability vector, while balanced accuracy depends only on the argmax. Both metrics stay close to their no-skill baselines (0.333 for balanced accuracy, 1.017 for log-loss), which suggests the available pitch characteristics carry limited information about the pitch result.

## 4.d: Naive Bayes Classification Rigor
**Assumptions:** 
```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Naive Bayes feature set, categorical features, Gaussian numerics
nb_vars <- c("pitch_name", "balls", "strikes", "stand", "p_throws",
             "release_speed", "release_spin_rate", "pfx_x", "pfx_z")
nb_train <- training_df %>% mutate(balls = factor(balls), strikes = factor(strikes))
nb_test  <- testing_df  %>% mutate(balls = factor(balls, levels = levels(nb_train$balls)),
                                   strikes = factor(strikes, levels = levels(nb_train$strikes)))

# Fit Naive Bayes with Laplace smoothing
nb_fit <- naiveBayes(Y ~ ., data = nb_train[, c("Y", nb_vars)], laplace = 1)
P_nb   <- predict(nb_fit, nb_test[, nb_vars], type = "raw")   # soft posteriors, columns = Ball, Strike, InPlay
colnames(P_nb) <- classes
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=7, fig.align="center"}
# Density plots 
training_df %>%
  select(Y, release_speed, release_spin_rate, pfx_x, pfx_z) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Y) %>%
  mutate(name = factor(name,
                       levels = c("release_speed", "release_spin_rate", "pfx_x", "pfx_z"),
                       labels = c("Release speed (mph)", "Spin rate (rpm)",
                                  "Horizontal break (ft)", "Vertical break (ft)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value, colour = Y)) + geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, title = "Density Plots of Numerical Predictors",
       colour = "Pitch result")
```

Naive Bayes assumes the features are conditionally independent given the pitch result. Numeric features (velocity, spin rate, horizontal and vertical break) follow Gaussian class-conditional densities. Categorical features (pitch type, balls, strikes, batter side, pitcher hand) use class-conditional frequency tables.

In the density plots above, each show one numeric predictor, with one curve representing one pitch result. In every density plot, all lines almost completely overlap in every panel. If a ball, a strike, and ball put in play pitch all have nearly the same velocity, spin, and break distributions, those features can barely tell the classes apart. 

Another thing to note is that the density curves are not Gaussian, or Normal. Vertical break (pfx_z) and release speed (release_speed) are bimodal and horizontal break (pfx_x) is pretty bumpy. The best distribution is release spin rate (release_spin_rate), which has a dominant peak, but is not completely smooth.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Conditional-independence check, correlation among the numeric predictors
num_cor <- round(cor(training_df[, c("release_speed", "release_spin_rate", "pfx_x", "pfx_z")]), 2)
rownames(num_cor) <- colnames(num_cor) <- pretty[colnames(num_cor)]

# Correlation table
kable(num_cor, caption = "Correlation among numeric predictors.")
```

Looking at the correlation table, most pairs are close to zero. The exception is release_speed and pfx_z, which have a value of 0.72. This is likely because faster pitches tend to have more vertical movement. Since Naive Bayes treats the two features as independent evidence, it essentially counts the same information twice. That tends to make its probabilities more extreme than they should be, which the calibration plot should show.

Given the information above, we suggest that there is not independence within the data. 

**Zero-frequency problem:** 

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Zero-frequency check, empty cells in the training data
nb_cat_vars <- c("pitch_name", "balls", "strikes", "stand", "p_throws")
zero_check <- data.frame(
  Feature = pretty[nb_cat_vars],
  `Empty cells` = sapply(nb_cat_vars, function(v) sum(table(nb_train[[v]], nb_train$Y) == 0)),
  check.names = FALSE)

kable(zero_check, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Zero-frequency check, empty feature-level-by-class cells.")
```

Every categorical feature (pitch type, balls, strikes, batter side, pitcher hand) was checked for feature-level-by-class combinations with no training observations, and found none. Regardless, we used Laplace smoothing (laplace = 1) so that a feature level never seen with a class in training cannot force that class's posterior to exactly zero. We extracted both the hard predicted classes (argmax of the posterior) and the soft posteriors $\hat{P}(Y = k \mid X)$.

**Hard Predicted Classes and Soft Posteriors:** 
```{r, echo = FALSE}
# Hard classes and soft posteriors for Naive Bayes
pred_nb <- max.col(P_nb, ties.method = "first")

# First 6 test pitches
post_tab <- data.frame(Actual = testing_df$Y, round(P_nb, 3), Predicted = classes[pred_nb])[1:6, ]
kable(post_tab, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Naive Bayes soft posteriors $\\widehat{P}(Y = k \\mid X)$ and hard predicted class for the first six test pitches.")
```

Looking each actual pitch in the table above gives us a lot of information about the model. For row 1, the pitch was Strike. The model gave an estimated probability of 0.395, which is only slightly bigger than InPlays probability of 0.384. While the model predicted Strike correctly, since both Strike and InPlay are so close together, there is low confidence in this prediction. For row 2, the pitch was Ball but was predicted to be Strike. This happened because the model gave Strike the biggest probability of 0.586, which is much bigger than predicting Ball (0.263). 

The model predicted 3 out of the first 6 test pitches. Further, the individual row probabilities of Ball, Strike, and InPlay stay close to their training proportions (Table 1), except InPlay in row 1. In other words, the posteriors are staying very close to their priors. Further, the model predicted Strike 5 out of the 6 times. This is because of the large prior Strike proportions (0.481). With such a large prior, Strike will win the argmax most often. 

## 4.d Comparing kNN & Naive Bayes
```{r, echo=FALSE}
P_null <- matrix(as.numeric(pi_train), nrow = nrow(testing_df), ncol = K,
                    byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(NULL, classes))
pred_null <- rep(which.max(pi_train), length(yte))

# Evaluate one model on the test set (multi-class)
eval_model <- function(P, y, pred) {
  n <- length(y)
  tab <- table(Pred = factor(pred, 1:K), Actual = factor(y, 1:K))
  tp <- diag(tab);  rs <- rowSums(tab);  cs <- colSums(tab)
  rec <- tp / cs
  prec <- ifelse(rs > 0, tp / rs, 0)
  f1 <- ifelse(prec + rec > 0, 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec), 0)
  po <- sum(tp) / n;  pe <- sum(rs * cs) / n^2
  den <- sqrt((n^2 - sum(rs^2)) * (n^2 - sum(cs^2)))
  Y1 <- diag(K)[y, ]
  c(Accuracy = po,
    BalancedAcc = mean(rec),
    MacroF1 = mean(f1),
    MCC = ifelse(den > 0, (sum(tp) * n - sum(rs * cs)) / den, 0),
    Kappa = (po - pe) / (1 - pe),
    LogLoss = multi_log_loss(y, P),
    Brier = mean(rowSums((P - Y1)^2))) 
}

res <- rbind("No-skill baseline" = eval_model(P_null, yte, pred_null),
             "kNN" = eval_model(P_knn,  yte, pred_knn),
             "Naive Bayes" = eval_model(P_nb,   yte, pred_nb))
res <- cbind(res, LL_Improvement = 1 - res[, "LogLoss"] / res["No-skill baseline", "LogLoss"])
```

**Confusion Matrices**
```{r, echo=FALSE,fig.align="center", results='asis'}
# Confusion matrices
cm_knn <- table(predicted = factor(classes[pred_knn], levels = classes),
                actual = factor(classes[yte], levels = classes))
cm_nb <- table(predicted = factor(classes[pred_nb], levels = classes),
                actual = factor(classes[yte], levels = classes))

kable(cm_knn, caption = paste0("kNN (k* = ", k_star, ") confusion matrix. Rows = predicted, columns = actual."))
kable(cm_nb, caption = "Naive Bayes confusion matrix. Rows = predicted, columns = actual.")
```

Looking at both confusion matrices of kNN and Naive Bayes, both models most accurately predict Strike. For kNN, accuracy is 0.469, which is essentially the same as always guessing Strike (0.4667). Therefore, accuracy here is misleading. Its accuracy matches the baseline only because it predicts the majority class almost every time. 

A worthy note is that kNN does not predict InPlay at all. This is because of the large $k^*$ (201). While Naive Bayes was able to predict all three classes, it only predicted InPlay 63 times, and mostly wrong. 

```{r, echo =FALSE}
# Comparative evaluation table
comp <- t(res[, c("Accuracy", "BalancedAcc", "MCC", "LogLoss", "LL_Improvement", "Brier")])
rownames(comp) <- c("Accuracy", "Balanced accuracy", "MCC", "Log-loss",
                    "Log-loss improvement over null", "Brier score")

# Which model is better on each metric, lower is better for log-loss and Brier
lower_better <- c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
two <- comp[, c("kNN", "Naive Bayes")]
best_idx <- ifelse(lower_better, apply(two, 1, which.min), apply(two, 1, which.max))

comp_tab <- data.frame(Metric = rownames(comp), round(comp, 4),
                       `Better model` = colnames(two)[best_idx],
                       check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
kable(comp_tab,
      caption = "Comparative test-set evaluation.")
```

No-skill baselines: accuracy = No Information Rate, balanced accuracy = 1/3, MCC = 0, Brier = $1 - \sum_k \pi_k^2$.

**Log-loss from the predicted probabilites**
The table above includes the log-loss from the predicted probabilities. For log-loss, the lower the value the better. When compared to the null baseline model, kNN produces a smaller log-loss value while naive bayes grew. Therefore, by this metric, we suggest kNN is better.

**Null Baseline Entropy**
The table above also includes null baseline entropy. From the table above, kNN make a 1.0133 improvement from the null model, while Naive Bayes decreases by 1.7. Therefore, by this metric, we suggest kNN is better.

**Balanced Accuracy**
For balanced accuracy, the higher the number the better. kNN had a positive increased of 0.0137. On the other hand, Naive Bayes had a slightly bigger positive increase of 0.0144. Therefore, based off this metric, we can conclude that Naive Bayes is better.

**Matthews Correlation Coefficient**
MCC prefers a higher number. Looking at the table above, kNN had a positive difference of 0.0427 while Naive Bayes had a positive, but not as positive, difference of 0.0327. Therefore, based off this metric, kNN is better. 

**Brier Score**
We want the Brier score to be as low as possible, so ideally we want kNN and Naive Bayes to have a negative difference from the baseline. Looking at the table above, kNN barely changes from the null model and Naive Bayes make a positive difference Therefore, the no-skill model is the best. 

**Calibration Plots**
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.5, out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
# Calibration plots
calib_df <- function(P, y, model) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:K, function(j) {
    d <- data.frame(p = P[, j], obs = as.integer(y == j))
    d$bin <- cut(d$p, breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.05), include.lowest = TRUE)
    d %>% group_by(bin) %>%
      summarise(mean_pred = mean(p), obs_freq = mean(obs), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
      filter(n >= 20) %>% 
      mutate(class = classes[j], model = model)
  }))
}

cal <- rbind(calib_df(P_knn, yte, paste0("kNN")),
             calib_df(P_nb,  yte, "Naive Bayes"))
cal$class <- factor(cal$class, levels = classes)

ggplot(cal, aes(mean_pred, obs_freq, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() + geom_point(aes(size = n), alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ class) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Mean predicted probability", y = "Observed frequency", 
       title = "Calibration Plots of kNN and Naive Bayes",
       colour = NULL, size = "Pitches") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The plots above represent the calibration plots, showing whether the predicted probability really corresponds to that class happening. 

For Ball, Naive Bayes predicts about 0.68 at its upper end, but is has an observed frequency of roughly 0.49. In this case, Naive Bayes is over-confident kNN is better, with its upper end matching much closer to the observed frequency. 

For Strike, both kNN and Naive Bayes have much flatter lines than the observed frequency line. In other words, the predictions are too extreme in both directions. On the lower end of Naive Bayes, the predicted probability is much higher than the observed diagonal. 0.8 predicted probability compared to a .30 observed frequency. In this case, Naive Bayes is again over-confident. 

For InPlay, the lines follow the observed diagonal the best out of all the other classes. Although, on the upper end of Naive Bayes, the model appears to be slighly over-confident. 

In general, the kNN models better follows the observed frequency diagonal. The Naive Bayes model tends to wonder off towards then end of the lines. With this being said, for both models, most observations are concentrated in the middle of the model. 

# 5. Discussion & Real-World Implications
<!-- 
address the discussion prompts listed in Section 6.
--->
**Accuracy vs. log-loss discrepancies:**
Neither model achieved high accuracy in the classification example, but it still overstates how well they do. kNN's accuracy (0.469) is pretty close to the no-skill baseline of always getting a strike (0.481). Since Strike is the most common result, it will predict Strike almost every time, scoring respectable without any real skill. The confusion matrix (Table 8) confirms this because InPlay was never predicted.

Naive Bayes shows overconfidence. While it is similar to kNN in that its accuracy (0.452) is near the no-skill baseline (0.481), its log-loss (1.0413) is worse than the no-skill baseline (1.0241). This is because log-loss penalizes a confident wrong probability heavily. Referencing back to the Calibration plots in 4.d, there was an 0.8 predicted probability compared to a .30 observed frequency for Strike. 

Accuracy only counts whether the top class is right, while log-loss does not. In this analysis of kNN and Naive Bayes, accuracy was inflated by class imbalance for kNN and masked overconfident errors for Naive Bayes. This is why we based k* and our comparison on log-loss and other metrics rather than accuracy alone.

**Generative vs. non-parametric trade-offs:**
Compared to Naive Bayes, kNN gave the better probability estimates. Its log-loss (1.0133) is better than the no-skill baseline, while Naive Bayes was worse (1.0413). The only metric in which Naive Bayes out-performed kNN was balanced accuracy (0.3477). Even then, kNN was only off by 0.0007. With that being said, Naive Bayes was the only model to predict all three classes, while kNN did not predict InPlay. 

The conditional independence assumption definitely hindered the performance of Naive Bayes. Velocity and vertical break were strongly correlated (0.72), so Naive Bayes ends up treating the same information twice. This ends up pushing the posteriors to the extremes, making it overconfident. 

Overall, kNN is non-parametric and makes no distributional assumption, but it needs its neighborhood size tuned and depends on the scaling and encoding choices. Naive Bayes is fast, needs no tuning, and is easy to interpret, but its assumptions are only approximately true here. However, in both cases, the predictors carry little signal about the pitch result, limiting both models. In the end, the kNN model is better because it is finer tuned and calibrated.
